steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for our paper on how self-supervised speech representations affect automatic assessment of dysarthric speech, covering the background on dysarthria, the gap in SSL research, and our contribution.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Dysarthria and why classification matters; data limitations
- SSL in speech processing and the research gap
- Our contribution: evaluation tool, tasks, noise scenarios

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Dysarthria
  - caused by lack of articulatory control, muscle weakness
  - affects speech rate, dynamic amplitudes, pitches, pronunciation
  - -> unintelligible speech; inaccurate articulation of phonemes, abnormal speech patterns
  - classification important: diagnosis, treatment options, speech therapy sessions
  - but: samples hard to get, most datasets have few speakers
  - limited research on performance insights for individual patients
- SSL and gap
  - SSL: learns from large, unlabeled datasets; better understanding of diverse speech patterns
  - SSL outperforms supervised in dysarthric Automatic Speech Recognition
  - not evaluated for other assessments: disease, word, intelligibility classification; various noise patterns
  - need to examine SSL across assessments and environment conditions
  - better understanding of impairments -> better tools for identifying disorders and traits
- Contribution
  - evaluate SSL representations (trained on large scale healthy speech), three noise scenarios, three classification tasks
  - tool: representations (acoustics, self-supervised) x classifiers (Logistic Regression (LR), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)), binary + multi-class
  - settings: default, noise addition, noise reduction (simulate real-world recording)
  - insight on features for identifying disorders and characteristics
  - e.g. severity classification: SSL extractors pretrained on healthy speech still perform well on dysarthric speech

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Dysarthria is caused by a lack of articulatory control and by muscle weakness. This affects speech rate, dynamic amplitudes and pitches, and how words are pronounced. All of this leads to unintelligible speech, and it is hard to understand because phonemes are articulated inaccurately and the speech patterns are abnormal. Classifying dysarthria has become more and more important for diagnosing the disorder, for finding the best treatment options, and for doing speech therapy sessions when they are needed. But it is usually hard to get dysarthric speech samples, since most datasets only have a small number of speakers. Also, there is not much research on how well these assessments can give specific performance insights for individual patients.

Self-Supervised learning (SSL) in speech processing makes it possible to learn from large, unlabeled datasets, which improves the understanding of diverse speech patterns. Recent research showed that SSL approaches can do better than supervised ones in dysarthric Automatic Speech Recognition, but SSL has not been evaluated for other dysarthric assessments, namely disease, word and intelligibility classification, and under different noise patterns. Because of this gap we need to look at SSL approaches in different dysarthric assessments and environment conditions. If we understand the types of impairments and their patterns better, this can help develop better tools for identifying disorders and their traits.

- Contribution
  - evaluate SSL representations (trained on large scale healthy speech), three noise scenarios, three classification tasks
  - tool: representations (acoustics, self-supervised) x classifiers (Logistic Regression (LR), Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)), binary + multi-class (disease, word, intelligibility)
  - settings: default, noise addition, noise reduction (simulate real-world recording)
  - insight on features for identifying disorders and characteristics
  - e.g. severity classification: SSL extractors pretrained on healthy speech still perform well on dysarthric speech

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Dysarthria is caused by a lack of articulatory control and by muscle weakness. This affects speech rate, dynamic amplitudes and pitches, and how words are pronounced. All of this leads to unintelligible speech, and it is hard to understand because phonemes are articulated inaccurately and the speech patterns are abnormal. Classifying dysarthria has become more and more important for diagnosing the disorder, for finding the best treatment options, and for doing speech therapy sessions when they are needed. But it is usually hard to get dysarthric speech samples, since most datasets only have a small number of speakers. Also, there is not much research on how well these assessments can give specific performance insights for individual patients.

Self-Supervised learning (SSL) in speech processing makes it possible to learn from large, unlabeled datasets, which improves the understanding of diverse speech patterns. Recent research showed that SSL approaches can do better than supervised ones in dysarthric Automatic Speech Recognition, but SSL has not been evaluated for other dysarthric assessments, namely disease, word and intelligibility classification, and under different noise patterns. Because of this gap we need to look at SSL approaches in different dysarthric assessments and environment conditions. If we understand the types of impairments and their patterns better, this can help develop better tools for identifying disorders and their traits.

Our main contribution is evaluating representations extracted by Self-Supervised models that were trained on large scale healthy speech, under three noise scenarios and across three classification tasks. We propose a tool to empirically evaluate different representations (e.g., acoustics and self-supervised methods) and classifiers (e.g., Logistic Regression (LR) and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)) on binary and multi-class tasks (e.g., disease, word, and intelligibility classification). We experiment under three settings, default, noise addition and noise reduction, to simulate how recordings are collected in the real world. Our tool can give insight into which features can help identify disorders and their characteristics. For example, for severity classification under the three scenarios, we showed that SSL feature extractors pretrained on healthy speech can be used on dysarthric speech and still give good performance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Dysarthria is caused by a lack of articulatory control and muscle weakness, which affect speech rate, dynamic amplitudes and pitches, and how the spoken word is pronounced. All of these contribute to unintelligible speech and difficulty understanding, due to the inaccurate articulation of phonemes and abnormal speech patterns [1]. Dysarthria classification has become increasingly important for diagnosing the disorder, determining the best treatment options, and conducting speech therapy sessions as needed [2]. However, obtaining dysarthric speech samples is usually challenging, as most datasets contain only a small number of speakers. Furthermore, there is limited research on how well these assessments can provide specific performance insights for individual patients.

Self-Supervised learning (SSL) in speech processing enables learning from large, unlabeled datasets, enhancing the understanding of diverse speech patterns [3]. While recent research has shown that SSL approaches can outperform supervised ones in dysarthric Automatic Speech Recognition [4,5], SSL has not been evaluated for other dysarthric assessments (disease, word and intelligibility classification) or under various noise patterns. This research gap underscores the need to examine SSL approaches in different dysarthric assessments and environment conditions. A better understanding of the types of impairments and their patterns can aid in developing better tools for identifying disorders and their traits.

Our main contribution is the evaluation of representations extracted by Self-Supervised models trained on large scale healthy speech under three noise scenarios, across three classification tasks. We propose a tool to empirically evaluate different representations (e.g., acoustics and self-supervised methods) and classifiers (e.g., Logistic Regression (LR) and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)) on binary and multi-class tasks (e.g., disease, word, and intelligibility classification). To simulate real-world recording collection scenarios, we experiment under three settings: default, noise addition, and noise reduction. Our tool can provide insight into which features can facilitate the identification of disorders and their characteristics. For instance, for severity classification under these three scenarios, we showed that SSL feature extractors pretrained on healthy speech can be applied to dysarthric speech and still provide good performance.

References:
[1] Viviana Mendoza Ramos, Charlotte Paulyn, Leen Van den Steen, Maria E Hernandez-Diaz Huici, Marc De Bodt, and Gwen Van Nuffelen, “Effect of boost articulation therapy (bart) on intelligibility in adults with dysarthria,” International Journal of Language & Communication Disorders , vol. 56, no. 2, pp. 271–282, 2021.
[2] Zhengjun Yue, Erfan Loweimi, Heidi Christensen, Jon Barker, and Zoran Cvetkovic, “Dysarthric Speech Recognition From Raw Waveform with Parametric CNNs,” in Proc. Interspeech , 2022, pp. 31–35.
[3] Wei-Ning Hsu, Benjamin Bolte, Yao-Hung Hubert Tsai, Kushal Lakhotia, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, and Abdelrahman Mohamed, “Hubert: Self-supervised speech representation learning by masked prediction of hidden units,” IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing , vol. 29, pp. 3451–3460, 2021.
[4] Zhaopeng Qian, Kejing Xiao, and Chongchong Yu, “A survey of technologies for automatic dysarthric speech recognition,” EURASIP Journal on Audio, Speech, and Music Processing , p. 48, 2023.
[5] Lester Phillip Violeta, Wen Chin Huang, and Tomoki Toda, “Investigating Self-supervised Pretraining Frameworks for Pathological Speech Recognition,” in Proc. Interspeech , 2022, pp. 41–45.
